paragraphs.heading: A protein that finds targets
paragraphs.text: An antibody, also called an immunoglobulin (Ig), is a large protein that the immune system uses to find and neutralize antigens, such as those on bacteria and viruses. The word antigen blends "antibody generator", and antigens of almost any size or chemical makeup can be recognized. Each antibody recognizes one or more specific antigens.

paragraphs.heading: How it grabs its target
paragraphs.text: An antibody is shaped roughly like a Y. The tip of each arm carries a paratope, the binding site, which fits exactly one epitope, the particular part of an antigen it latches onto. Once bound, the antibody can tag the antigen, or a microbe or infected cell carrying it, for attack by immune cells. It can also neutralize the target directly, for example by blocking the part of a virus it needs to invade a host cell. So that the immune system can recognize millions of different antigens, paratopes come in an equally wide variety.

paragraphs.heading: The parts of the Y
paragraphs.text: Antibodies are heavy proteins of about 150 kDa and about 10 nm in size, made of three globular regions. In humans and most other mammals, one antibody unit has four polypeptide chains, joined by disulfide bonds: a matching pair of heavy chains and a matching pair of light chains. The two arms are the antigen-binding fragments (Fab), and the trunk of the Y is the crystallisable fragment (Fc). A flexible hinge between them lets antibodies grab pairs of epitopes at different distances and bind effector molecules more easily.

paragraphs.heading: Five classes
paragraphs.text: Apart from the tips, the rest of an antibody varies much less. Human antibodies fall into five classes, also called isotypes, named IgA, IgD, IgE, IgG and IgM, and IgG and IgA are split further into subclasses. The class decides which functions the antibody sets off, called effector functions, and also where in the body and at what stage of a response it is released. Classes with the same name can behave differently in other species: mouse IgG1 works more like human IgG2 than human IgG1.

paragraphs.heading: Where antibodies come from
paragraphs.text: Antibodies are made by antibody-secreting cells, a term covering plasmablasts and plasma cells. During an immune response, B cells can develop into these cells or into memory B cells. Plasmablasts multiply fast and live briefly, and they appear early in a response. Plasma cells do not divide, yet they release huge amounts of antibody whether or not antigen is around, and long-lived ones can potentially survive for the organism's whole life, classically in niches in the bone marrow.

paragraphs.heading: Part of adaptive immunity
paragraphs.text: Antibodies are generally counted as part of the adaptive immune system. They are highly specific, they are produced through genetic rearrangements rather than being written directly in the germline, and they reflect immunological memory. Memory B cells can last for decades and be called up quickly in a second response. The picture is not perfectly tidy, though: natural IgM, made by B-1 cells, recognizes many unrelated antigens and works with the complement system early in a response, acting more like innate immunity.
